title: Geodesic-based optimal control for leakage suppression in superconducting qubits
authors: Adonai Hilário da Silva, Tanmoy Pandit, Francesco Cosco
abstract: Superconducting qubits are often based on the first two energy levels of a physical anharmonic LC oscillator. Since the anharmonicity of such systems is usually much lower than the involved energy gaps, population can easily leak to higher energy states. This is what characterizes leakage errors, and it can have multiple sources: from coherent error induced by the control platform to incoherent thermal dissipation. In this work, we adapt an optimal control method based on sub-Riemannian geodesic search in the unitary group for a system consisting of two superconducting qubits with leakage levels. We use the $R_x(π/2)$ rotation for single-qubit operation analysis, and the $i$SWAP operation for two-qubit analysis. For the former, we find considerable performance improvement in average gate fidelity as well as in the reduction of leakage errors when comparing the obtained optimal pulses with Gaussian and DRAG pulses, especially for short duration pulses. For the $i$SWAP gate, although leakage error remains roughly the same, we manage to obtain considerably higher fidelities with the cost of requiring a slightly longer time evolution.
summary: This paper develops an advanced optimal control technique based on geodesic search to mitigate leakage errors in superconducting qubits. By smoothly shaping control pulses and deriving an effective Hamiltonian, the authors demonstrate significant improvements in gate fidelity over existing methods for both single- and two-qubit operations. This advances the practical viability of superconducting quantum hardware.
main_problem: The primary goal is to suppress leakage errors in superconducting qubits during quantum gate operations, which arise from population leaking to higher energy states.
main_result: The proposed geodesic-based optimal control method significantly improves average gate fidelity and reduces leakage errors for single-qubit rotations compared to standard pulses, while achieving higher fidelity for two-qubit gates at the cost of slightly longer evolution times.
method: The authors adapt an optimal control technique using sub-Riemannian geodesic search on the unitary group, incorporating an envelope function to ensure smooth control pulse turn-on and turn-off.
model_or_system: The system models two superconducting qubits coupled via a tunable coupler, treated as anharmonic LC oscillators. The dynamics are governed by a full Hamiltonian, which is then simplified using Schrieffer-Wolff and Rotating-Wave Approximations to derive an effective Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Average gate fidelity, leakage error rate, and the resulting unitary operation U(τ).
important_parameters: Qubit frequencies, anharmonicities, coupling strengths, and the specific control pulse parameters (e.g., for $R_x(\pi/2)$ and iSWAP gates).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the coupler remains in its ground state (Schrieffer-Wolff) and applies the Rotating-Wave Approximation (RWA) to simplify the Hamiltonian.
paper_structure: The paper first reviews the geodesic optimal control formalism and introduces leakage noise mitigation. It then details the physical model for two coupled qubits, deriving the effective Hamiltonian through sequential approximations (SW, RWA). Finally, it presents simulation results comparing the optimal pulses to standard pulses.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical hardware limitation (leakage) in superconducting quantum processors by merging advanced concepts from optimal control theory (differential geometry) with solid-state quantum physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 2. Effective coupling constants of Eq. (28) as a function of the frequency of the tunable coupler. The gray dashed vertical lines indicate the values for which each coupling is null. The optimal value for minimal interaction is ωc/(2π) = 7.945 GHz, for which we get |Γ↓↓| and |Γ↑↑| in the order of 240 Hz, and |Γ↓↑| = |Γ↑↓| ≈4 Hz. For the time scale of single- qubit gates, these values correspond to the two qubits being effectively decoupled. For the iSWAP interaction, we select ωc/(2π) = 5.862 GHz, which is still comfortably within the dispersive regime while allowing for exchange interactions.

FIG. 3. Single-qubit pulses resulting in the Rx(π/2) rotation operation with gate time τ for 24 different values ranging from τ = 14 ns to τ = 38 ns. The curves are shown with decreasing opacity as the pulse duration increases. Inset we highlight the specific 17 ns pulse. In dashed blue we show −(1/α)dΩx(t)/dt, showing that the geodesic optimal pulse does not result in Ωy(t) proportional to the first derivative of Ωx(t), differently from DRAG pulses.

FIG. 4. Average infidelity, leakage, and seepage rates as functions of the duration of a single-qubit Rx(π/2) pulse using different pulse types. The shaded grey area corresponds to the limit set by the simulated thermal dissipation process. The optimized pulses through the geodesic search method show values for the three analyzed quantities minimized to the limit set by thermal dissipation even for short pulses.

FIG. 5. Single-qubit pulses applied on each qubit for the synthesis of an iSWAP two-qubit gate. Since the optimization is done in the frame co-rotating with the two- qubits’ frequencies, the oscilations indicate the applied pulses must be off-resonant with the qubits.

FIG. 6. Average infidelity for the iSWAP operation as function of evolution time. In complete absence of any signal from the control line, an iSWAP with F = 0.9548 is achieved at t = 79.5 ns. By turning on the control line with the geodesic optimized pulses, it is possible to synthesize the iSWAP with F = 0.9942 at t = 86 ns. The shaded grey area corresponds to the limit set by the simulated thermal dissipation process. The two vertical lines only indicate precisely the values in time τoff = 79.5 ns and τon = 86 ns for which the infidelity is minimum.
